The **mayor of Paris** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Maire de Paris_[[mɛʁ d(ə) paʁi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")[chief executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") of [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), the capital and largest city in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France").
The officeholder is responsible for the administration and management of the city, submits proposals and recommendations to the [Council of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Paris "Council of Paris"), is active in the enforcement of the city's ordinances, submits the city's annual budget and appoints city officers, department commissioners or directors, as well as members of city boards and commissions. During meetings of the Council of Paris, the mayor serves as the presiding officer, as it is the case in any other [commune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communes_of_France "Communes of France") in France. Since Paris doubles as a [department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_France "Departments of France") as well, the mayor also has the rank of a [departmental council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departmental_council_\(France\) "Departmental council \(France\)") president.
Since 29 March 2026, [Emmanuel Grégoire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Gr%C3%A9goire "Emmanuel Grégoire") of the [Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\) "Socialist Party \(France\)") has been the Mayor of Paris.
## History
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayor_of_Paris&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]
When the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution") began after the [storming of the Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storming_of_the_Bastille "Storming of the Bastille") on 14 July 1789, the city insurgents murdered the last [Provost of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provost_of_Paris "Provost of Paris") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%A9v%C3%B4t%20de%20Paris "fr:Prévôt de Paris")] ([Provost of the Merchants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provost_of_the_Merchants?action=edit&redlink=1 "Provost of the Merchants \(page does not exist\)") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%A9v%C3%B4t%20des%20marchands%20de%20Paris "fr:Prévôt des marchands de Paris")]), [Jacques de Flesselles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_de_Flesselles "Jacques de Flesselles"). Because the Provost's office was abolished as one of the first moves with the dissolution of the _[Ancien Régime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancien_R%C3%A9gime "Ancien Régime")_ , the insurgents established a revolutionary government called the "[Commune of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Commune_\(French_Revolution\) "Paris Commune \(French Revolution\)")", initially led by [Jean Sylvain Bailly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Sylvain_Bailly "Jean Sylvain Bailly"), the first titled "Mayor of Paris". The mayor's office was very important during the critical phases of the Revolution, and during [Robespierre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilien_Robespierre "Maximilien Robespierre")'s [Reign of Terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Terror "Reign of Terror") (1793–1794) it was decisive in the discovery and execution of all suspected [counter-revolutionaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-revolutionaries "Counter-revolutionaries"). In July 1794, after the [9th Thermidor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermidorian_Reaction "Thermidorian Reaction"), the [coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d'%C3%A9tat "Coup d'état") that deposed and executed Robespierre and his cronies, the office of Mayor was abolished since it was perceived to be too powerful.
After the [February Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_Revolution "February Revolution") of 1848, the [July Monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_Monarchy "July Monarchy") ended in favor of a [new Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Second_Republic "French Second Republic"), that restored the mayor's office. This renewal was however short, as the [June Days uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_Days_uprising "June Days uprising") of the same year ended the possibility of creating a strong mayorship. The [Executive Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Executive_Commission_\(1848\) "French Executive Commission \(1848\)")—charged to provisionally rule the country—preferred to transfer the mayor's powers to the [Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine_\(department\) "Seine \(department\)") [Prefect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefect_\(France\) "Prefect \(France\)"), appointed by [Ministry of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_the_Interior_\(France\) "Minister of the Interior \(France\)").
In 1870, once again, the office of Mayor of Paris was re-established and again did not survive long. The occasion for the re-creation was the fall of the [Second Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Second_Empire "French Second Empire") after the defeat in the [Franco-Prussian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War "Franco-Prussian War"). The provisional [Government of National Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_National_Defense "Government of National Defense") of [Louis-Jules Trochu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Jules_Trochu "Louis-Jules Trochu") believed that a strong leadership in Paris would prevent sedition during the [Prussian siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Paris_\(1870%E2%80%9371\) "Siege of Paris \(1870–71\)"). After the definitive conquest of Paris by Prussians, popular discontent erupted in a new insurrectionary [Commune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Commune "Paris Commune") which held [socialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist "Socialist") beliefs. Also, in case the Commune was finally suppressed, the [new national government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_French_Republic "Third French Republic") preferred to divide Paris into several distinct mayorships (one for each [arrondissement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrondissements_of_Paris "Arrondissements of Paris")) to prevent the city's total loss in the event of further revolts.
Thus, for all but 14 months from 1794 to 1977, Paris was the only [commune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communes_of_France "Communes of France") of France without a mayor, and had less autonomy than even the smallest village. For most of the time from 1800 to 1977 (except briefly in 1848 and 1870–71), it was controlled directly by the departmental prefect (the prefect of the Seine before 1968 and prefect of Paris after 1968). In 1975 [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Parliament "French Parliament") passed a bill re-establishing an elected mayor for Paris, beginning in 1977. The bill was signed by [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France "President of France") [Valéry Giscard d'Estaing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val%C3%A9ry_Giscard_d'Estaing "Valéry Giscard d'Estaing") on 31 December 1975. In March 1977, after the first formal [municipal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1977_French_municipal_elections "1977 French municipal elections"), former Prime Minister [Jacques Chirac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Chirac "Jacques Chirac") was chosen as Mayor of Paris, a position he held until 1995, when he was elected [President of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France "President of France").
